services.h1: Cat Spaying — Protecting Your Cat From Preventable Disease
services.lead: Spaying removes the ovaries and uterus, eliminating heat cycles, unwanted pregnancies, and the risk of life-threatening uterine infections.
services.body:
What Is Spaying?

Spaying (ovariohysterectomy) is the surgical removal of a female cat's ovaries and uterus. It's performed under general gas anaesthesia and is one of the most frequently performed procedures at our clinic.

Why Spaying Matters

  • Eliminates the risk of pyometra — a life-threatening uterine infection common in unspayed cats
  • Removes the risk of ovarian and uterine cancer entirely
  • Significantly reduces the risk of mammary tumours, especially if done before the first heat cycle
  • Stops heat-cycle yowling, restlessness, and escape attempts
  • Prevents unwanted litters

What to Expect at Shivraj Pet Clinic

We recommend spaying before the first heat cycle (typically 5-6 months) for the strongest protection against mammary tumours, though we safely spay cats of any age. Surgery takes 30-40 minutes, with same-day discharge in most cases and a suture check 10 days later.

Common Signs to Watch For

  • Loud yowling or restlessness (heat cycle)
  • Frequent attempts to escape outdoors
  • Discharge from the vulva
  • Lethargy with loss of appetite
  • Abdominal swelling (possible pyometra)

faqs.q: When should I spay my cat?
faqs.a: Before the first heat cycle, usually around 5-6 months, gives the strongest protection against mammary tumours later in life.

faqs.q: My cat already had kittens — is it too late to spay?
faqs.a: No. Spaying is beneficial at any age and still removes future pregnancy and uterine disease risk.

faqs.q: How long does recovery take?
faqs.a: Most cats are back to normal within 7-10 days. We recommend an e-collar to prevent licking the incision.

faqs.q: Is this the same as a hysterectomy in humans?
faqs.a: Similar in concept — we remove both the uterus and ovaries, which is more thorough than ovary-only sterilization and prevents uterine disease entirely.

services.lead: A thorough, unhurried examination is the foundation of good medicine. Dr. Pritesh takes the time to examine every system, understand the history, and explain the findings clearly.
services.body:
What Happens at a Consultation

At Shivraj Pet Clinic & Lab, every consultation follows a structured approach that leaves nothing to chance. Dr. Pritesh reviews the history, performs a complete physical examination from nose to tail, and integrates findings from any diagnostics run the same day.

You receive a clear, honest explanation of what was found, what it means, what the treatment options are, and what to watch for at home. We don't rush appointments and we encourage questions — because an informed pet owner is the most important part of any treatment plan.

What Conditions Are Commonly Treated?

Dermatology (Skin & Coat)

  • Allergic skin disease — food allergies, environmental atopy, flea allergy dermatitis
  • Pyoderma (bacterial skin infection)
  • Mange — Demodex and Sarcoptes mite infestations
  • Ringworm (dermatophytosis)
  • Hot spots (acute moist dermatitis)
  • Seborrhoea and scaling conditions

Gastrointestinal

  • Vomiting and diarrhea — acute and chronic
  • Pancreatitis
  • Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)
  • Constipation and megacolon in cats
  • Parvovirus and other intestinal infections
  • Liver disease — hepatitis, fatty liver, portosystemic shunts

Respiratory

  • Kennel cough (infectious tracheobronchitis)
  • Pneumonia — bacterial, viral, fungal
  • Feline upper respiratory complex (cat flu)
  • Tracheal collapse in small breeds
  • Pleural effusion (fluid around lungs)

Urinary

  • Urinary tract infections (UTI)
  • Feline lower urinary tract disease (FLUTD)
  • Urinary blockage in male cats — emergency
  • Chronic kidney disease (CKD) management
  • Bladder stones

Endocrine / Hormonal

  • Diabetes mellitus — insulin management in dogs and cats
  • Cushing's disease (hyperadrenocorticism)
  • Hypothyroidism in dogs
  • Hyperthyroidism in cats
  • Addison's disease

Neurological

  • Seizures — diagnosis and long-term management
  • Disc disease and spinal pain
  • Vestibular disease (sudden head tilt and loss of balance)
💊 Second opinions welcome: If your pet has received a diagnosis elsewhere that you're unsure about, Dr. Pritesh is happy to review records, repeat examination, and provide an independent assessment. We encourage it — good medicine benefits from scrutiny.

faqs.q: What does a consultation cost at Shivraj Pet Clinic?
faqs.a: Consultation fee is ₹300, payable at the clinic. All costs for diagnostics or treatment are discussed and agreed upfront — no surprise bills.

faqs.q: Can I come without an appointment?
faqs.a: Walk-ins are accepted during clinic hours. For complex cases or if you want to ensure a specific time slot, calling ahead is recommended. Emergencies are always seen immediately.

faqs.q: Do you treat cats and exotic animals, not just dogs?
faqs.a: Yes — Dr. Pritesh treats dogs, cats, birds, rabbits, turtles, guinea pigs, hamsters, and other exotic species. We're one of the few clinics in PCMC with this range of expertise.

faqs.q: What if my pet needs multiple tests the same day?
faqs.a: We prefer to complete diagnostics in one visit where possible. Our in-house lab, X-ray, and ultrasound mean most diagnostic workups can be done same-day without referral.

faqs.q: Can I get a second opinion from Dr. Pritesh on a serious diagnosis?
faqs.a: Absolutely. We encourage second opinions for cancer, neurological disease, organ failure, and any condition where the diagnosis will significantly change the pet's management. Bring previous records and we'll review them honestly.

services.h1: CT Scan & MRI for Pets — Referral Coordination, Pune
services.lead: When your pet needs advanced cross-sectional imaging, we coordinate referral to trusted facilities. Dr. Pritesh guides you through the process and ensures continuity of care.
services.body:
When Standard Imaging Isn't Enough

X-ray and ultrasound are powerful diagnostic tools but have limitations. Complex neurological cases, surgical planning for tumours, detailed fracture assessment, and cancer staging sometimes require cross-sectional imaging — the ability to see structures in three dimensions.

When CT or MRI is required, Shivraj Pet Clinic coordinates referral to trusted imaging facilities in Pune. Dr. Pritesh reviews the results directly and guides all subsequent treatment decisions, so your pet's care remains seamless throughout.

When CT or MRI Is Recommended

Neurological Conditions

  • Spinal disc disease (IVDD) — identifying the exact disc and degree of compression before surgery
  • Brain conditions — size, location, and extent assessment
  • Spinal fractures and instability
  • Wobbler syndrome in large breed dogs

Surgical Planning

  • Complex fracture reconstruction — 3D visualisation of fragment position
  • Chest and abdominal tumour surgery — mapping involvement of blood vessels and organs
  • Nasal and sinus conditions — detailed extent mapping

Cancer Staging

  • Lung metastasis screening
  • Lymph node assessment
  • Abdominal organ involvement

Supported Species

  • Dogs
  • Cats
  • Rabbits
  • Birds
  • Turtles
📋 Seamless referral process: We prepare a detailed referral summary, share all relevant in-house diagnostic results, and remain your primary contact throughout — so your pet is never just a number at an unfamiliar facility.

faqs.q: Do you have CT or MRI on-site?
faqs.a: No. CT and MRI are arranged through referral centres when required. We coordinate the referral, share all relevant records, and guide you through the process so there is no delay in your pet's care.

faqs.q: When would you recommend CT or MRI over X-ray?
faqs.a: When X-ray shows a problem but doesn't provide enough detail for a definitive diagnosis or surgical plan. Neurological cases such as disc disease or paralysis, complex fractures, and cancer staging are the most common indications.

faqs.q: My dog has a slipped disc — does it need CT or MRI?
faqs.a: Not always. Mild disc cases often respond to medical management without advanced imaging. If surgery is being considered or neurological signs are severe, CT or MRI helps identify the exact location and severity to guide surgical planning.

services.h1: Digital X-Ray for Pets — Instant On-Site Results in Pimple Nilakh
services.lead: High-resolution digital radiography for bones, chest, abdomen, and soft tissue. Results available immediately — no waiting, no referrals.
services.body:
Why Digital X-Ray Matters

X-ray (radiography) is one of the most important diagnostic tools in veterinary medicine. It lets us see inside your pet's body without surgery — assessing bones, joints, chest, and abdominal organs with immediate, high-resolution images.

At Shivraj Pet Clinic, we use digital radiography rather than old film X-ray. Digital X-ray produces sharper images, can be enhanced on-screen, and is ready within seconds — not minutes. Dr. Pritesh reviews images immediately and discusses findings with you before you leave.

What X-Ray Diagnoses

Bone & Joint Conditions

  • Fractures — from road accidents, falls, trauma
  • Hip dysplasia — malformed hip joint, common in large breed dogs
  • Elbow dysplasia and OCD (Osteochondrosis Dissecans)
  • Spinal disc disease (IVDD) — disc bulges causing back pain or paralysis
  • Bone tumors and cancer lesions
  • Patellar luxation (kneecap slipping)
  • Arthritis — joint space narrowing, bone remodeling

Chest Conditions

  • Pneumonia and lung infections
  • Pleural effusion (fluid around the lungs)
  • Heart enlargement and congestive heart failure
  • Tracheal collapse in small breed dogs
  • Lung masses and metastatic cancer

Abdominal Conditions

  • Bladder stones — visible on X-ray if calcium-containing
  • Kidney stones and kidney enlargement
  • Intestinal obstruction — from swallowed objects
  • GDV (bloat) — the characteristic gas-filled stomach pattern
  • Splenic masses
  • Pregnancy — puppy/kitten count, foetal positioning

Exotic Animals

We use digital X-ray for rabbits, birds, turtles, and guinea pigs — adapted for their small size. This allows us to diagnose fractures, respiratory disease, egg binding, and bladder stones in exotic patients that cannot be diagnosed by examination alone.

📋 X-ray and bloodwork together: For most sick pets, we combine X-ray with blood panels from our in-house lab. Together they give Dr. Pritesh a complete picture — structural (X-ray) and biochemical (blood) — leading to a faster, more accurate diagnosis.

faqs.q: Is X-ray safe for my pet?
faqs.a: Yes. Digital X-ray uses a very low dose of radiation. The exposure for a routine veterinary X-ray is minimal and the risk is negligible compared to the diagnostic benefit of getting an accurate diagnosis.

faqs.q: Does my pet need to be sedated for X-ray?
faqs.a: Many pets can be X-rayed without sedation if they are calm and the area being imaged cooperates. For anxious pets, uncooperative positioning, or painful conditions where movement would be harmful, light sedation gives us clearer images and is safer for the patient.

faqs.q: Can you do X-ray on rabbits and birds?
faqs.a: Yes — we regularly X-ray rabbits, birds, and guinea pigs. Exotic patients are handled with extra care and positioned specifically for their anatomy.

faqs.q: How quickly will I get results?
faqs.a: Digital X-ray images are available within seconds on our monitor. Dr. Pritesh reviews and explains findings before you leave the clinic in most cases.

services.h1: Dog Neutering — Safe, Same-Day Surgery in Pimple Nilakh
services.lead: A routine procedure that reduces aggression, roaming, and the risk of testicular and prostate disease in male dogs.
services.body:
What Is Dog Neutering?

Neutering (castration) is the surgical removal of a male dog's testicles, performed under general anaesthesia. It's one of the most common and safest procedures in veterinary medicine, typically completed within 30-45 minutes with the dog going home the same evening.

Why Pet Owners Choose Neutering

  • Eliminates the risk of testicular cancer entirely
  • Significantly reduces prostate problems in older age
  • Reduces marking, mounting, and roaming behaviour
  • Often reduces aggression toward other male dogs
  • Helps control the local stray dog population

What to Expect at Shivraj Pet Clinic

We use gas anaesthesia rather than older injectable-only protocols — it's safer for the heart and lungs, and dogs recover alertness faster. Pre-surgery bloodwork is done in our in-house lab the same morning, so there's no waiting on outside results before we operate. Most dogs go home within a few hours of surgery, with a 10-14 day recovery and a follow-up suture check included.

Common Signs to Watch For

  • Roaming or escaping to find mates
  • Mounting behaviour
  • Urine marking indoors
  • Aggression toward other male dogs
  • Visible testicular swelling or asymmetry

faqs.q: What age should I get my dog neutered?
faqs.a: Most vets, including ours, recommend neutering between 6 and 9 months of age, though we evaluate larger breeds case by case since some benefit from waiting until closer to a year.

faqs.q: Will neutering change my dog's personality?
faqs.a: It typically reduces roaming, marking, and male-to-male aggression, but won't change a dog's core temperament or playfulness.

faqs.q: How long is recovery?
faqs.a: Most dogs are back to normal activity within 10-14 days. We provide an e-collar and pain medication, and a follow-up check is included.

faqs.q: Is anaesthesia safe for older dogs?
faqs.a: We run pre-anaesthetic bloodwork on every patient, especially seniors, using our in-house lab to assess organ function before surgery.

services.lead: Found a lump on your dog? Most skin masses are benign, but early evaluation and removal give the best outcome either way.
services.body:
Why Lumps Need Evaluation, Not Just Watching

Not every lump is cancer — many are benign lipomas, cysts, or warts. But the only way to know for certain is examination, and in some cases, a needle aspirate or biopsy. We never recommend surgery on a guess; we diagnose first, then decide together whether removal is needed.

What Is the Treatment Process?

  • Step 1 — Physical exam: we assess size, location, growth rate, and firmness
  • Step 2 — Fine needle aspirate: a quick, low-discomfort sample examined under our in-house microscope, often same-visit
  • Step 3 — Surgical removal if indicated: performed under gas anaesthesia with margins assessed during surgery
  • Step 4 — Pathology: for any mass with cancer risk, we send tissue for histopathology to confirm complete removal

What About Mammary Tumors Specifically?

Mammary tumors are common in unspayed female dogs, especially over age 7. Roughly half are malignant in dogs, which is why we evaluate promptly rather than waiting. Spaying significantly reduces this risk in the first place — see our Dog Neutering & Cat Spaying pages.

Common Signs to Watch For

  • New lump or bump anywhere on the body
  • A lump that's growing or changing shape
  • Bleeding or ulceration on a mass
  • Multiple lumps along the mammary chain
  • A lump your dog licks or chews at

faqs.q: Is every lump cancer?
faqs.a: No — most skin lumps in dogs turn out to be benign (lipomas, cysts, warts). But size, location, and growth speed all matter, which is why we examine rather than guess.

faqs.q: Do you need to biopsy before surgery?
faqs.a: For many masses, a quick needle aspirate during the same visit gives us enough information to plan surgery. Full biopsy after removal confirms the diagnosis.

faqs.q: How big can a mass be before it's a problem?
faqs.a: Size matters less than behaviour — a small, fast-growing, firm, or ulcerated mass is more concerning than a large, slow-growing, soft one. We'll tell you honestly which category yours falls into.

faqs.q: Will my dog need chemotherapy after surgery?
faqs.a: Most benign and many malignant masses need only surgical removal. We'll discuss further treatment only if pathology results indicate it's necessary.

services.h1: Emergency Surgery — When Every Hour Matters
services.lead: If your pet has been hit by a vehicle, is bleeding heavily, can't breathe normally, or has a swollen, painful abdomen — call us immediately.
services.body:
Call First, Always

If you suspect a true emergency, call +91 77569 65169 before you travel — we'll tell you what to do on the way and prepare the surgical team if needed. Don't wait to see if symptoms improve on their own.

Conditions That Need Immediate Surgical Attention

  • Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) — a swollen, hard abdomen in dogs is a life-threatening emergency
  • Severe trauma from vehicle accidents or falls
  • Internal bleeding (pale gums, weakness, collapse)
  • Deep penetrating wounds or impalement injuries
  • Difficulty breathing combined with chest trauma
  • Dystocia (difficult birth) requiring emergency C-section

What We Do On Arrival

Emergency cases are assessed immediately on arrival — vital signs, pain stabilization, and rapid in-house diagnostics (X-ray, ultrasound, bloodwork) to identify the problem without delay. If surgery is needed, we move directly into the operating suite. Having lab, imaging, and surgical capability all on-site means we're not sending you elsewhere to wait for answers during a crisis.

Common Signs to Watch For

  • Hard, swollen abdomen with retching but nothing coming up
  • Pale or white gums
  • Collapse or inability to stand
  • Heavy bleeding that won't stop with pressure
  • Severe difficulty breathing
  • Visible bone or open fracture after trauma

faqs.q: Are you open for emergencies on Wednesday (your day off)?
faqs.a: Wednesday is our scheduled weekly off for routine visits, but call the clinic number for any true emergency — we will guide you on next steps.

faqs.q: What is GDV and why is it so urgent?
faqs.a: GDV (bloat) is when the stomach fills with gas and twists on itself, cutting off blood supply. It progresses within hours and is fatal without emergency surgery — a hard, swollen abdomen with unproductive retching needs immediate attention.

faqs.q: Should I try to treat bleeding at home first?
faqs.a: Apply firm direct pressure with a clean cloth while traveling to us, but don't delay the trip to experiment with home remedies — call us en route so we're ready when you arrive.

faqs.q: Do you have in-house diagnostics for emergencies?
faqs.a: Yes — X-ray, ultrasound, and lab bloodwork are all on-site, so we can identify the problem within minutes of arrival rather than waiting on outside results.

services.h1: Exotic Pet Veterinary Care in Pune — Rabbits, Birds, Turtles & More
services.lead: One of the very few clinics in PCMC with dedicated equipment and clinical experience for birds, rabbits, turtles, reptiles, and small exotic mammals.
services.body:
Why Exotic Pets Need a Specialist

Exotic animals are not small dogs. Their anatomy, metabolism, disease patterns, and response to anaesthesia are completely different from cats and dogs — and most general veterinary clinics in Pune simply don't have the training, equipment, or experience to treat them safely.

At Shivraj Pet Clinic & Lab, Dr. Pritesh Vidhate has extensive clinical experience treating exotic pets including rabbits, birds, turtles and small mammals. With hands-on experience treating hundreds of exotic patients every year, we use species-appropriate gaseous anaesthesia, species-specific diagnostic protocols, and individualized treatment plans for every exotic patient.

Which Animals Do We Treat?

  • 🐰 Rabbits — GI stasis, dental disease, neutering/spaying, respiratory infections
  • 🦜 Parrots & Birds — African Greys, Macaws, Budgies, Cockatiels, Finches, Lovebirds
  • 🐢 Turtles & Tortoises — Shell infections, metabolic bone disease, Vitamin A deficiency
  • 🦎 Reptiles & Iguanas — Skin infections, nutritional disorders, parasite treatment
  • 🐹 Hamsters & Gerbils — Wet tail, overgrown teeth, cheek pouch impaction
  • 🐾 Guinea Pigs — Dental malocclusion, scurvy (Vitamin C deficiency), skin conditions

What Services Are Available for Exotic Pets?

  • Health Checkups — Species-specific wellness exams, weight monitoring, behavioral assessment
  • Diagnostic Testing — In-house blood panels, X-ray, ultrasound adapted for small exotic patients
  • Nutritional Guidance — Correct diets for each species (most exotic pet illness is diet-related)
  • Surgical Procedures — Rabbit neutering/spaying with safe gaseous anaesthesia, abscess drainage
  • Grooming & Maintenance — Beak trimming, nail clipping for birds; dental rasping for rabbits
  • Disease Treatment — GI stasis in rabbits, egg binding in birds, shell rot in turtles
  • Emergency Care — Exotic animals can deteriorate rapidly; we attend urgent cases during clinic hours

Common Conditions We Treat

  • GI Stasis in Rabbits — The most common life-threatening rabbit emergency. Gut stops moving. Immediate treatment required.
  • Egg Binding in Birds — Female birds unable to pass an egg. Painful, rapidly fatal without veterinary intervention.
  • Shell Rot in Turtles — Bacterial or fungal infection of the shell, often secondary to poor housing conditions.
  • Metabolic Bone Disease — Calcium deficiency in reptiles and turtles from incorrect diet or lighting.
  • Wet Tail in Hamsters — Severe diarrhea, often fatal within 48 hours without treatment.
  • Dental Malocclusion in Rabbits & Guinea Pigs — Overgrown or misaligned teeth causing inability to eat.
  • Avian Respiratory Disease — Breathing difficulties, tail bobbing, open-mouth breathing in birds.
⚠️ Exotic pets hide illness: By the time a rabbit, bird, or turtle shows obvious symptoms, the condition is often serious. If your exotic pet seems quieter than usual, eats less, or sits in a corner — that's enough reason to call us.

faqs.q: Is it safe to anesthetize a rabbit or bird for surgery?
faqs.a: Yes, when done correctly with gaseous anaesthesia and species-specific protocols. We use safe inhalation anaesthesia — the same approach used in specialist exotic animal hospitals. Injectable-only anaesthesia is far riskier in small exotics, and we avoid it.

faqs.q: My rabbit hasn't eaten in 12 hours — is that serious?
faqs.a: Yes. Rabbits that stop eating for more than 6–8 hours can develop GI stasis, which becomes life-threatening within 24 hours. Call us immediately if your rabbit stops eating or producing droppings.

faqs.q: Can you treat my turtle for shell problems?
faqs.a: Yes. We treat shell rot, soft shell (metabolic bone disease), and shell injuries. We also provide advice on correct housing, UVB lighting, and calcium supplementation to prevent recurrence.

faqs.q: My bird is sitting fluffed up at the bottom of the cage — what should I do?
faqs.a: This is a serious warning sign. Sick birds hide illness until they can no longer compensate. A bird sitting low and fluffed is often in respiratory distress or severely ill. Call us immediately.

faqs.q: Do you neuter rabbits in Pune?
faqs.a: Yes — rabbit neutering (castration for males, spaying for females) is one of the procedures Dr. Pritesh performs regularly using gaseous anaesthesia. Spaying is particularly important for female rabbits because over 80% of unspayed females develop uterine cancer by age 5.

services.h1: Foreign Body Removal — When Your Pet Swallows Something They Shouldn't
services.lead: Toys, socks, string, bones, stones — pets swallow things that can block or tear the intestines. Fast diagnosis prevents a small problem becoming a fatal one.
services.body:
Why This Is More Common Than You'd Think

Dogs and cats — especially puppies, kittens, and naturally curious breeds — frequently swallow objects that can't pass through the digestive tract. Common culprits we see: socks, string or thread (especially dangerous in cats), small toy parts, fruit pits, and bones that splinter.

How We Diagnose It

If you've seen your pet eat something concerning, or they're showing symptoms without a known cause, we start with a same-visit digital X-ray. Many objects (bone, metal, dense plastic) show up clearly. For items that don't show on X-ray, like fabric or thread, we use in-house ultrasound to look for the secondary signs — bunched intestines, obstruction patterns, or fluid buildup.

What Are the Treatment Options?

Not every swallowed object needs surgery. Small, smooth objects sometimes pass naturally and we may monitor with repeat imaging. Sometimes an object can be removed endoscopically if it's still in the stomach. But if it's caused an obstruction or has moved into the intestines, surgical removal (enterotomy) is needed — and the timeline matters, since a blocked or torn intestine becomes an emergency.

Common Signs to Watch For

  • Repeated vomiting, especially right after eating or drinking
  • Loss of appetite lasting more than a day
  • Visible straining with little or no stool
  • Lethargy combined with abdominal discomfort
  • You directly witnessed your pet eat a non-food item

faqs.q: My dog ate a sock yesterday and seems fine — should I still bring them in?
faqs.a: Yes, get them checked. Some objects sit in the stomach for days before causing a blockage, and catching it on X-ray before symptoms worsen is far safer than waiting.

faqs.q: My cat keeps trying to swallow string — why is this dangerous?
faqs.a: String and thread are uniquely dangerous in cats because one end can anchor (often under the tongue) while the rest is pulled into the intestines, causing a sawing injury internally. This is always an urgent case — call us right away.

faqs.q: Will my pet need surgery every time they swallow something?
faqs.a: Not always — size, shape, and location matter. We'll image first and give you an honest assessment of whether monitoring, endoscopy, or surgery is the right call.

faqs.q: How can I prevent this from happening again?
faqs.a: We'll talk through specific prevention strategies for your pet's habits during the visit — often it's about what's left within reach rather than a behavioural issue to "fix."

services.h1: Orthopedic Surgery — Fractures, Ligaments & Joint Care
services.lead: From a fall, an accident, or wear over time — broken bones and torn ligaments need fast, accurate diagnosis and skilled surgical repair.
services.body:
What Conditions Do We Treat?

  • Limb fractures from falls, road accidents, or trauma
  • Fracture repair — bone plating and intramedullary pinning
  • Ligament injuries and joint surgery
  • Patellar luxation (kneecap slipping out of place), common in small breeds
  • Hip dysplasia and joint degeneration in older pets
  • Dislocations following trauma

Why Imaging Comes First

We never operate on a guess. Digital X-ray gives us a clear view of bone alignment and fracture pattern same-visit. For complex cases requiring more detailed cross-sectional imaging, we coordinate referral to trusted facilities so surgical planning is accurate and complete.

What Is the Surgical Approach?

Depending on the injury, repair may involve pinning, plating, external fixation, or ligament reconstruction. All orthopedic procedures are done under gas anaesthesia with full vital monitoring. Recovery includes pain management and a structured activity-restriction plan — we'll walk you through exactly what your pet can and can't do during healing.

Common Signs to Watch For

  • Sudden limping or refusing to bear weight
  • Visible swelling around a joint or limb
  • Yelping when a leg is touched
  • Limb held at an unusual angle after a fall
  • Gradual worsening lameness in older pets

faqs.q: My dog suddenly won't put weight on a leg — what could it be?
faqs.a: Sudden limping may result from a fracture, ligament injury, spinal issue, sprain, or soft tissue trauma. Prompt veterinary examination is recommended — call us and describe what you are seeing.

faqs.q: Can small fractures heal without surgery?
faqs.a: Some hairline fractures in small bones can be managed with strict rest and splinting. We'll tell you honestly whether your pet's specific fracture needs surgical fixation based on the X-ray.

faqs.q: How long is recovery from orthopedic surgery?
faqs.a: Recovery depends on the condition and procedure performed. Most orthopedic patients require several weeks of restricted activity, pain management, and follow-up examinations. We provide a clear recovery plan tailored to your pet.

faqs.q: Do you have CT scan available?
faqs.a: CT imaging is arranged through referral centres when required. We coordinate the process and ensure all records are shared so there is no delay in your pet's care.

services.lead: No referrals. No waiting days for results. Our in-house laboratory processes blood panels, urinalysis, and cytology on-site — with CBC and biochemistry results ready in 15–20 minutes, so treatment starts the same visit.
services.body:
Why an In-House Lab Changes Everything

Most veterinary clinics in Pune send samples to external labs and wait 24–48 hours for results. At Shivraj Pet Clinic & Lab, serving Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, our fully-equipped in-house pathology laboratory processes the majority of routine tests within the same visit. This means Dr. Pritesh can see your pet's results, diagnose the condition, and begin treatment — all before you leave the clinic.

For sick or emergency patients, this speed is critical. A dog in suspected tick fever, a rabbit with suspected organ failure, a bird with an unclear diagnosis — in each case, waiting a day for lab results can be the difference between full recovery and a critical decline.

What Tests Are Available In-House?

Complete Blood Count (CBC)

Measures red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Essential for detecting anaemia, infection, inflammation, clotting problems, and bone marrow disorders.

Biochemistry Profile

Assesses organ function through blood chemistry markers:

  • Liver enzymes (ALT, AST, ALP) — detect liver inflammation, damage, toxin exposure
  • Kidney values (BUN, Creatinine) — essential for detecting chronic kidney disease early
  • Blood glucose — diagnoses diabetes mellitus in dogs and cats
  • Protein levels (Albumin, Total Protein) — assess nutrition and organ function
  • Electrolytes (Sodium, Potassium, Chloride) — critical in vomiting, diarrhea, Addison's disease

Urinalysis

Urine analysis reveals kidney function, urinary tract infections, bladder crystals/stones, diabetes, and early kidney disease — often before blood values change. We examine urine dipstick, specific gravity, sediment under microscope.

Microscopy & Cytology

  • Skin scraping — detects mange mites (Demodex, Sarcoptes), ringworm
  • Ear cytology — identifies yeast, bacteria causing ear infections
  • Fine needle aspirate (FNA) — evaluates lumps and masses without surgery
  • Vaginal cytology — determines heat cycle stage in breeding animals
  • Fecal microscopy & examination — identifies intestinal parasites, Giardia, Coccidia

Parasite & Infectious Disease Screening

  • Tick fever testing — Ehrlichia, Babesia, Anaplasma rapid tests
  • PCR Testing — for accurate detection of infectious diseases
  • Fecal float and direct smear for intestinal parasites
  • Blood smear for blood parasites

Specialised Tests

  • Bird Feather DNA Testing
  • Pre-anaesthetic bloodwork for surgery safety
🔬 Pre-anaesthetic screening: Before any surgery, we run bloodwork to assess liver, kidney, and clotting function. This is not optional — it's what makes anaesthesia safe, especially for senior pets and exotic animals.

faqs.q: How long do blood test results take?
faqs.a: CBC and biochemistry reports are generally available within 15–20 minutes in most routine cases at our in-house lab. We aim to have results ready before you leave the clinic.

faqs.q: Does my healthy pet need blood tests?
faqs.a: Yes — annual wellness bloodwork for pets over 7 years, and before any surgery regardless of age. Many conditions (kidney disease, diabetes, liver disease) show no symptoms until advanced. Early detection changes outcomes dramatically.

faqs.q: Do you send any tests to external labs?
faqs.a: Histopathology (tissue biopsy) and some specialized culture tests go to external labs. We'll tell you upfront which tests need to go out and what the turnaround time is.

faqs.q: My pet needs surgery — why does it need blood tests first?
faqs.a: Pre-anaesthetic blood panels reveal hidden kidney or liver problems that affect how the body processes anaesthetic drugs. A pet that appears healthy can still have borderline organ function that requires us to adjust our protocol for safety.

faqs.q: Can you test for tick fever?
faqs.a: Yes — we have rapid in-house tests for the most common tick-borne diseases in Pune (Ehrlichiosis, Babesiosis, Anaplasmosis). Results in 15–20 minutes.

services.title: Pet Vaccination in Wakad & Pimple Saudagar | Shivraj Pet Clinic
services.description: Complete pet vaccination and preventive medicine at Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad, Pimple Saudagar & Pune. Dogs, cats, rabbits, and exotic pets. Call 077569 65169.
services.h1: Pet Vaccination & Preventive Care in Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune
services.lead: Prevention is the most powerful medicine. From core vaccines to parasite protection — keeping your pet healthy before illness strikes.
services.body:
Why Preventive Care Matters

Most serious diseases that affect dogs and cats in Pune are entirely preventable with timely vaccination and routine health checks. Parvovirus, distemper, rabies, and feline panleukopenia kill hundreds of pets in PCMC every year — and the majority of these deaths happen in unvaccinated animals.

At Shivraj Pet Clinic & Lab in Pimple Nilakh, our preventive medicine program is designed to catch problems before they become emergencies. Regular wellness visits give Dr. Pritesh the chance to detect early signs of organ disease, dental problems, skin conditions, and joint issues that owners rarely notice at home.

What Is the Vaccination Schedule?

In India, annual vaccination is recommended for most pets. Schedules are tailored to your pet's age, lifestyle, travel and health status.

Vaccination schedules are customised based on age, lifestyle, travel and health status. Consult Dr. Pritesh for a personalised plan.

Deworming & Parasite Prevention

Parasites are extremely common in Pune's climate — roundworms, tapeworms, and hookworms affect dogs and cats of all ages. Ticks are endemic in Wakad, Pimple Saudagar, and surrounding areas and can transmit fatal diseases like Ehrlichiosis and Babesiosis within 24 hours of attachment.

  • Puppy & Kitten Deworming — Starting at 2 weeks of age, repeated every 2 weeks until 3 months
  • Adult Deworming — Every 3–6 months depending on lifestyle and risk
  • Tick & Flea Prevention — Parasite prevention is recommended based on your pet's age, lifestyle and health status. Our veterinarians will advise the most suitable option during consultation.
  • Parasite Screening — Stool examination for active worm burden, recommended annually

What Happens During a Wellness Examination?

A yearly wellness exam is the single most effective thing you can do for a pet that looks and acts healthy. Dr. Pritesh examines every organ system — eyes, ears, teeth, skin, lymph nodes, heart, lungs, abdomen — and can identify problems at a stage when they're far easier and less expensive to treat.

  • Puppy & Kitten Health Checks — Growth monitoring, developmental milestones, diet guidance
  • Adult Annual Wellness — Physical exam, vaccination review, parasite check, nutritional assessment
  • Senior Pet Wellness (7+ years) — Blood panel, organ function, joint assessment, dental grade
  • Preventive Bloodwork — CBC and biochemistry to detect diabetes, kidney disease, liver disease early
  • Dental Health Assessment — Grading dental disease, recommending cleaning schedules
💡 Shivraj Pet Clinic tip: Many serious conditions in senior pets — kidney disease, diabetes, liver disease — show no symptoms until they're advanced. A simple annual blood panel at our in-house lab catches these at a treatable stage.

faqs.q: What age should I start vaccinating my puppy?
faqs.a: Puppies should start their first vaccination at 6–8 weeks of age. The core series runs until 16 weeks, with a booster at 1 year. We'll give you a complete schedule at your first visit.

faqs.q: How often does my adult dog need vaccines?
faqs.a: In India, annual vaccination is recommended for most pets. Vaccination schedules may vary based on age, lifestyle, travel, boarding requirements and health status. Dr. Pritesh will advise a personalised plan during your visit.

faqs.q: My cat stays indoors — does it still need vaccines?
faqs.a: Yes. Indoor cats can still be exposed to infectious diseases through visitors, other pets, and contaminated objects brought into the home. Annual vaccination remains important.

faqs.q: What tick prevention product do you recommend for Pune?
faqs.a: Parasite prevention recommendations are based on your pet's age, lifestyle, and medical history. Our veterinarians will advise the most suitable option during your consultation.

faqs.q: Can I deworm my pet at home without a vet?
faqs.a: Over-the-counter dewormers only cover some worm types. A stool test tells us exactly what parasite is present so we can treat it accurately. We recommend a proper parasite screening at least once a year.

services.title: Soft Tissue Surgery | Wakad & Pimple Saudagar | Shivraj
services.description: Expert soft tissue surgery for dogs, cats and exotic pets at Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad, Pimple Saudagar & Pune. Call 077569 65169.
services.h1: Soft Tissue Surgery — Wounds, Hernias & Internal Repair
services.lead: Beyond bones — surgical care for skin, organs, and internal structures, from a torn wound to an abdominal repair.
services.body:
What Procedures Fall Under This Category?

  • Wound repair and reconstruction following injury or dog fights
  • Hernia correction (umbilical, inguinal, perineal)
  • Cherry eye and eyelid surgery
  • Abscess drainage and surgical cleaning
  • Anal gland surgery for recurring impaction
  • Bladder and abdominal organ procedures

Why Quick Evaluation Matters

Soft tissue injuries can look minor on the surface but involve deeper damage that's only clear on examination. A small skin tear might need only cleaning and stitches; a deeper wound near the abdomen needs imaging to rule out internal injury before we proceed. We assess every case individually rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach.

Anaesthesia & Recovery

Most soft tissue procedures are done under general gas anaesthesia for patient comfort and surgical precision, with local/sedation options for minor cases where appropriate. Recovery time varies by procedure — we'll give you a specific timeline and aftercare plan for your pet's exact surgery.

Common Signs to Watch For

  • Open wound that won't stop bleeding or oozes
  • Visible bulge near the belly button or groin (possible hernia)
  • Red, swollen lump near the eye
  • Persistent licking or scooting near the tail base
  • Foul-smelling discharge from a swollen area (possible abscess)

faqs.q: My dog has a hernia — is this urgent?
faqs.a: Some hernias are stable and can be scheduled; others (especially if the bulge becomes hard, painful, or discolored) need same-day attention since tissue can become trapped. Call us and describe what you're seeing and we'll advise.

faqs.q: Will a wound need stitches or can it heal on its own?
faqs.a: Depends on depth and location — we'll examine and tell you honestly whether it needs surgical closure or will heal fine with cleaning and bandaging.

faqs.q: What is cherry eye and does my dog need surgery?
faqs.a: Cherry eye is a prolapsed gland in the third eyelid, common in certain breeds. It usually requires a minor surgical repositioning procedure rather than removal, to preserve normal tear production.

services.title: Pregnancy Ultrasound in Wakad & Pimple Saudagar | Shivraj Pet Clinic
services.description: On-site pregnancy ultrasound for dogs and cats at Shivraj Pet Clinic, Wakad, Pimple Saudagar & Pune. Early, safe pregnancy confirmation and foetal heartbeat detection. Call 077569 65169.
services.h1: Pregnancy Ultrasound & Sonography in Wakad & Pimple Saudagar, Pune
services.lead: Non-invasive, real-time pregnancy confirmation for dogs and cats. Ultrasound detects foetal heartbeats and gives an early, safe way to confirm pregnancy well before it's visible.
services.body:
What Ultrasound Shows That X-Ray Cannot

X-ray and ultrasound are complementary tools. X-ray shows bones and gross size well but can't detect a pregnancy reliably until the skeleton calcifies, late in gestation. Ultrasound shows soft tissue directly and can detect a foetal heartbeat far earlier — giving a safe, real-time confirmation of pregnancy weeks before X-ray would show anything.

Pregnancy Ultrasound: What It Confirms

  • Pregnancy confirmation — foetal heartbeats visible from 21–25 days post-breeding
  • Puppy/kitten count — approximate litter size assessment
  • Foetal viability — assessing foetal distress or death before whelping
🩺 Why confirm early: Early pregnancy confirmation lets you plan nutrition, prepare for whelping, and catch a non-viable pregnancy or false pregnancy early — rather than waiting weeks for physical signs to appear.

faqs.q: Is ultrasound safe for pets?
faqs.a: Completely. Ultrasound uses sound waves — no radiation. It's safe for pregnant animals, foetuses, and can be repeated as many times as needed.

faqs.q: Does my pet need to be shaved for ultrasound?
faqs.a: A small area of fur is clipped for proper probe contact and image quality. The clip is minimal and grows back quickly.

faqs.q: Can you tell how many puppies my dog is carrying?
faqs.a: Yes — ultrasound confirms pregnancy from about 3 weeks post-breeding. Counting is approximate on ultrasound; X-ray at 45+ days gives a more accurate litter count.

faqs.q: My vet in another clinic said my dog has a heart murmur — what should I do?
faqs.a: We recommend consulting Dr. Pritesh who can examine your pet thoroughly and advise on the next steps, which may include referral for cardiac assessment if needed.

Why an In-House Pharmacy Matters

When a diagnosis is made, treatment should start immediately — not tomorrow, after a trip to a human pharmacy to hunt for a veterinary prescription. At Shivraj Pet Clinic & Lab, our in-house pharmacy stocks the complete range of medicines for dogs, cats, and exotic animals, allowing Dr. Pritesh to dispense prescription medicines directly at the consultation.

This is particularly important for acute conditions — a dog diagnosed with a urinary blockage, a cat with a severe respiratory infection, a rabbit with GI stasis — where same-day treatment is critical to outcomes.

What Medicines and Supplies Do We Stock?

Prescription Medicines

  • Antibiotics — a complete range for skin, urinary, respiratory, gastrointestinal, and systemic infections
  • Anti-inflammatory pain medication (NSAIDs) — post-surgery, arthritis, injury
  • Corticosteroids — allergy management, immune-mediated disease

  • Ear mite treatment
  • Mange treatment

Nutritional Supplements

  • Joint supplements (Glucosamine, Chondroitin, Omega-3) for arthritis
  • Liver support supplements (SAMe, Silymarin)
  • Probiotic and digestive enzyme supplements
  • Vitamin and mineral supplements for exotic animals
  • Kidney support diets and supplements

Specialty Items

💊 Dispensing only under prescription: All prescription medications are dispensed only after examination and diagnosis by Dr. Pritesh. We don't dispense prescription medicines without a clinical reason — this protects your pet and prevents antimicrobial resistance.

faqs.q: Can I buy tick prevention without a consultation?
faqs.a: Standard over-the-counter parasite control products (spot-ons, some tablets) can be purchased without a consultation. Prescription-only parasite control products (like some chewables) require a consultation first.

faqs.q: Do you sell therapeutic diets for kidney or liver disease?
faqs.a: Yes — we stock veterinary therapeutic diets for chronic kidney disease, liver disease, skin conditions, gastrointestinal disease, and obesity management.

faqs.q: Can you provide medicines for exotic pets like rabbits and birds?
faqs.a: Yes. We carry medications specifically dosed and formulated for exotic species, which often require different formulations than those used for dogs and cats.

faqs.q: My dog is on long-term medication — can I just pick it up without a new consultation each time?
faqs.a: For stable long-term conditions, we can arrange repeat dispensing after an initial assessment. However, annual or biannual check-ins are recommended to ensure the medication is still appropriate and the dose is correct.

faqGroups.heading: Dog Health FAQs — Pune Pet Parents Ask

items.q: My dog has stopped eating. Should I be worried?
items.a: Yes. If your dog refuses food for more than 24 hours, or sooner if accompanied by vomiting, diarrhoea, lethargy, or fever, a veterinary examination is recommended.

items.q: My dog is vomiting repeatedly. When should I visit the vet?
items.a: Repeated vomiting, especially with blood, weakness, or refusal to eat, requires prompt veterinary attention to prevent dehydration and identify the underlying cause.

items.q: Why does my dog have diarrhoea?
items.a: Diarrhoea can result from dietary indiscretion, parasites, infections, food allergies, or more serious diseases. Persistent diarrhoea should be evaluated by a veterinarian.

items.q: My dog is limping. Does it always need treatment?
items.a: Not always, but limping may indicate a sprain, fracture, ligament injury, arthritis, or paw injury. If it persists for more than 24 hours or is severe, veterinary examination is advised.

items.q: My dog is scratching all the time. What could be the reason?
items.a: Common causes include fleas, ticks, mites, allergies, bacterial infections, fungal infections, and hormonal disorders.

items.q: Why does my dog shake its head frequently?
items.a: Head shaking often indicates ear infections, ear mites, allergies, or foreign material inside the ear.

items.q: My dog has a lump. Should it be removed?
items.a: Not every lump requires surgery, but every new lump should be examined. Early diagnosis helps determine whether it is benign or cancerous.

items.q: When should I get my dog spayed or neutered?
items.a: The ideal age depends on breed, size, and overall health. Your veterinarian will recommend the most appropriate timing.

items.q: What is pyometra in female dogs?
items.a: Pyometra is a serious uterine infection in unspayed females and is a surgical emergency requiring immediate treatment.

items.q: My dog is having difficulty urinating. Is it an emergency?
items.a: Yes. Difficulty passing urine or complete inability to urinate is an emergency and requires immediate veterinary care.

items.q: Does my dog need dental cleaning?
items.a: Dogs with tartar, bad breath, bleeding gums, or loose teeth often benefit from professional dental cleaning under anaesthesia.

items.q: Why is my dog drinking excessive water?
items.a: Increased water intake may be associated with kidney disease, diabetes, hormonal disorders, liver disease, or certain medications.

items.q: What vaccinations does my dog need?
items.a: Vaccination schedules vary with age and lifestyle but commonly include protection against rabies, parvovirus, distemper, hepatitis, and leptospirosis.

items.q: How often should I deworm my dog?
items.a: Most adult dogs should be dewormed every three months, while puppies require more frequent deworming.

items.q: My dog has blood in its urine. What does it mean?
items.a: Blood in the urine may indicate urinary tract infection, bladder stones, trauma, or other urinary diseases and requires veterinary evaluation.

items.q: Can senior dogs undergo surgery safely?
items.a: Yes. With appropriate pre-operative testing, anaesthetic planning, and monitoring, many senior dogs safely undergo surgery.

items.q: What should I do if my dog has been hit by a vehicle?
items.a: Keep your dog as still as possible and seek emergency veterinary care immediately, even if injuries are not immediately visible.

items.q: Why is my dog coughing?
items.a: Coughing may be caused by kennel cough, heart disease, tracheal disorders, pneumonia, or other respiratory conditions.

items.q: Do you perform emergency surgeries for dogs?
items.a: Yes. Emergency procedures such as Caesarean section, foreign body removal, pyometra surgery, wound repair, and bladder surgery are performed when medically indicated at our Pimple Nilakh clinic.

items.q: Why choose Shivraj Pet Clinic for dog treatment?
items.a: We provide comprehensive medical, surgical, diagnostic, and emergency dog care in Wakad, Pimple Saudagar & PCMC, using modern equipment and evidence-based veterinary medicine.

faqGroups.heading: Cat Health FAQs — Pune Pet Parents Ask

items.q: My cat has stopped eating. Is it an emergency?
items.a: Yes. Cats that stop eating, especially for more than 24 hours, are at risk of serious complications such as hepatic lipidosis and should be examined promptly.

items.q: My cat cannot urinate. What should I do?
items.a: This is a life-threatening emergency, particularly in male cats. Immediate veterinary treatment is essential.

items.q: Why is my cat vomiting frequently?
items.a: Frequent vomiting may be caused by hairballs, dietary problems, kidney disease, gastrointestinal disorders, or other medical conditions.

items.q: My cat is hiding all the time. Is something wrong?
items.a: Cats often hide when they are in pain or unwell. Sudden behavioural changes should not be ignored.

items.q: Why is my cat losing weight despite eating?
items.a: Weight loss may be associated with hyperthyroidism, diabetes, intestinal disease, parasites, or cancer.

items.q: My cat has blood in its urine. What could be causing it?
items.a: Blood in the urine may result from feline lower urinary tract disease (FLUTD), urinary tract infections, bladder stones, or stress-related cystitis.

items.q: Does my cat need dental treatment?
items.a: Cats commonly develop dental disease, which may cause pain, bad breath, drooling, and difficulty eating. Professional dental care may be required.

items.q: Why is my cat breathing rapidly?
items.a: Rapid breathing may indicate respiratory disease, heart disease, pain, fever, or fluid around the lungs and requires immediate examination.

items.q: When should I spay or neuter my cat?
items.a: The recommended timing depends on your cat's age and health. Your veterinarian can advise the most appropriate age.

items.q: My cat has diarrhoea. Should I be concerned?
items.a: Persistent diarrhoea may be caused by parasites, infections, dietary intolerance, inflammatory bowel disease, or systemic illness.

items.q: Why is my cat drinking more water than usual?
items.a: Excessive thirst may indicate kidney disease, diabetes, hyperthyroidism, or other medical conditions.

items.q: My cat has a lump. Should it be checked?
items.a: Yes. Any new lump or swelling should be evaluated early to determine whether further treatment is needed.

items.q: What vaccinations does my cat need?
items.a: Core vaccinations typically include protection against feline panleukopenia, herpesvirus, calicivirus, and rabies, depending on lifestyle and local recommendations.

items.q: How often should my cat be dewormed?
items.a: Adult cats are generally dewormed every three months, while kittens require more frequent treatment.

items.q: My cat is drooling excessively. Is that normal?
items.a: Excessive drooling may indicate dental disease, oral ulcers, poisoning, nausea, or foreign bodies in the mouth.

items.q: Can older cats safely undergo surgery?
items.a: Yes. Many senior cats successfully undergo surgery after appropriate health assessment and anaesthetic planning.

items.q: Why is my cat straining in the litter tray?
items.a: Straining may indicate constipation, urinary blockage, bladder disease, or other serious conditions that require prompt veterinary care.

items.q: My cat is sneezing continuously. Does it need treatment?
items.a: Persistent sneezing may result from viral infections, allergies, nasal polyps, foreign bodies, or dental disease.

items.q: Do you perform surgery for cats?
items.a: Yes. We perform spaying, neutering, tumour removal, bladder surgery, foreign body removal, wound repair, soft tissue surgery, and other medically indicated procedures at our Pune clinic.

items.q: Why choose Shivraj Pet Clinic for cat treatment?
items.a: We provide dedicated feline medical and surgical care with modern diagnostics, in-house laboratory facilities, digital imaging, and personalised treatment plans for every cat in Wakad, Pimple Saudagar & Pune.

faqGroups.heading: Pet Bird FAQs — Budgies, Cockatiels, Parrots & More

items.q: Why is my bird sitting fluffed up all day?
items.a: A fluffed-up bird that remains inactive is often trying to conserve heat and energy. This is a common sign of illness and should be examined by an avian veterinarian as soon as possible.

items.q: Why has my bird stopped eating suddenly?
items.a: Birds have a very fast metabolism. Even a short period without eating can become life-threatening. Loss of appetite may be caused by infections, liver disease, digestive problems, or pain.

items.q: Is tail bobbing in birds normal?
items.a: No. Tail bobbing while breathing usually indicates respiratory distress or another serious illness and requires immediate veterinary attention.

items.q: Why is my bird breathing with its beak open?
items.a: Open-mouth breathing may indicate respiratory disease, overheating, or severe stress. Prompt examination is recommended.

items.q: My bird is bleeding. What should I do?
items.a: Keep your bird calm, apply gentle pressure with a clean cloth if possible, and seek veterinary care immediately. Birds can lose dangerous amounts of blood quickly.

items.q: Why are my bird's droppings green?
items.a: Green droppings may be associated with reduced food intake, liver disease, infections, or other medical conditions. A veterinary examination is needed to determine the cause.

items.q: Can birds undergo surgery safely?
items.a: Yes. With appropriate anaesthesia, monitoring, and surgical expertise, many birds can safely undergo necessary surgical procedures.

items.q: Why is my bird vomiting seeds?
items.a: Seed regurgitation or vomiting may indicate crop disorders, infections, toxins, or gastrointestinal disease and should not be ignored.

items.q: How often should my bird have a health check-up?
items.a: Healthy birds should ideally have a preventive health examination once a year, while older birds or those with medical conditions may require more frequent visits.

items.q: Do you treat all pet bird species?
items.a: Yes. We treat budgies, cockatiels, lovebirds, African greys, macaws, cockatoos, finches, canaries, and many other pet birds at our Pune Exotic Animal Centre.

items.q: Why is my turtle not eating?
items.a: Poor appetite can result from incorrect temperature, stress, infections, parasites, or metabolic disease. A veterinary examination can identify the underlying cause.

items.q: What is shell rot?
items.a: Shell rot is a bacterial or fungal infection of the shell that requires cleaning, medication, and correction of habitat conditions.

items.q: Why are my turtle's eyes swollen?
items.a: Swollen eyes are commonly caused by vitamin A deficiency, infections, or poor water quality.

items.q: Why is my turtle floating sideways?
items.a: Uneven floating may indicate pneumonia, excessive intestinal gas, or buoyancy disorders and should be evaluated by a veterinarian.

items.q: Does my turtle or tortoise need UVB lighting?
items.a: Yes. UVB light is essential for proper calcium metabolism, healthy bones, and shell development in both pet turtles and tortoises — glass and mesh both filter out UVB, so time behind either doesn't count.

items.q: Why is my turtle's shell soft, or my tortoise's shell bumpy?
items.a: A soft shell in turtles or a bumpy, pyramided shell in tortoises usually points to the same root cause — inadequate calcium, insufficient UVB, or an imbalanced diet during growth. Prevention through correct husbandry matters more than treatment once it's set in.

items.q: What should I feed my turtle or tortoise?
items.a: Diets differ by species — tortoises generally need mostly dark leafy greens with only occasional fruit, while aquatic turtles need a mix of pellets, greens, and protein. Ask us for a species-specific feeding ratio.

items.q: Can turtles and tortoises undergo surgery?
items.a: Yes. Surgical treatment may be required for reproductive disorders, shell injuries, abscesses, and certain internal conditions.

items.q: Does my tortoise need to hibernate in Pune's climate?
items.a: Most tortoises kept as pets in Pune don't need to hibernate given the mild winters, and unsupervised hibernation carries real risk. Talk to us before attempting it.

items.q: How often should turtles and tortoises be examined?
items.a: Annual health check-ups help detect nutritional deficiencies, shell problems, and internal diseases before they become severe.

items.q: What temperature and humidity does a pet iguana need?
items.a: Iguanas need a basking spot noticeably warmer than the rest of the enclosure, with humidity kept fairly high. Getting either wrong is one of the most common causes of illness we see in pet lizards.

items.q: What should I feed my pet iguana?
items.a: Iguanas are largely herbivorous and need a varied mix of leafy greens and vegetables with appropriate calcium supplementation — not the fruit-heavy or protein-heavy diets sometimes recommended online.

items.q: Why does my lizard's tail look darker or shrivelled at the tip?
items.a: This can indicate poor circulation, an old injury, or in some cases a retained shed. It's worth a veterinary look rather than waiting to see if it resolves on its own.

items.q: My lizard is having trouble shedding its skin — is that a problem?
items.a: Incomplete or difficult shedding is usually a sign that humidity in the enclosure is too low. Retained shed around toes or the tail tip can restrict blood flow if it isn't resolved, so it's worth addressing promptly.

items.q: Does my pet lizard need UVB lighting?
items.a: Yes, for the vast majority of common pet lizard species, including iguanas. Without proper UVB, they can't metabolise dietary calcium correctly, which leads to metabolic bone disease over time.

items.q: Do you treat lizards and other reptiles besides turtles?
items.a: Yes — our Exotic Animal Centre sees iguanas and other common pet lizards alongside turtles, tortoises, birds, and small mammals.

items.q: My rabbit has stopped eating. Is it an emergency?
items.a: Yes. Rabbits that stop eating can rapidly develop gastrointestinal stasis, which is a medical emergency requiring immediate treatment.

items.q: What is gastrointestinal stasis?
items.a: It is a condition where the digestive system slows or stops moving normally. Early treatment greatly improves the chances of recovery.

items.q: Should I spay or neuter my rabbit?
items.a: Yes. Spaying and neutering help prevent reproductive diseases, reduce unwanted behaviours, and improve long-term health.

items.q: At what age should rabbits be spayed or neutered?
items.a: The ideal age depends on the rabbit's breed, sex, weight, and health. Your veterinarian can recommend the best timing.

items.q: Why are my rabbit's teeth overgrowing?
items.a: Rabbit teeth grow continuously. Poor diet, genetics, or dental disease can prevent normal wear and lead to painful overgrowth.

items.q: Can rabbits safely undergo anaesthesia?
items.a: Yes. With proper pre-operative assessment and monitoring, rabbits can safely undergo many surgical procedures.

items.q: Why is my rabbit passing very small droppings?
items.a: Small droppings often indicate reduced gut movement or inadequate food intake and should be evaluated promptly.

items.q: Can rabbits develop uterine cancer?
items.a: Yes. Unspayed female rabbits have a high risk of uterine cancer as they age, making spaying an important preventive procedure.

items.q: What should rabbits eat daily?
items.a: Unlimited grass hay, fresh water, leafy vegetables, and a measured amount of quality pellets form the basis of a healthy rabbit diet.

items.q: Do you perform rabbit surgeries?
items.a: Yes. We perform rabbit spays, neuters, tumour removal, wound repair, dental procedures, and other surgical treatments at our Pimple Nilakh clinic.

items.q: Why has my guinea pig stopped eating?
items.a: Guinea pigs should never go long without eating. Loss of appetite may indicate dental disease, pain, digestive problems, or other serious illnesses.

items.q: Why do guinea pigs need vitamin C?
items.a: Unlike humans, guinea pigs cannot produce vitamin C. A deficiency can cause weakness, joint pain, poor wound healing, and other health problems.

items.q: Can guinea pigs develop bladder stones?
items.a: Yes. Bladder stones are relatively common and may cause pain, blood in the urine, or difficulty urinating.

items.q: Why is my guinea pig losing weight?
items.a: Weight loss may result from dental disease, chronic illness, infections, parasites, or inadequate nutrition.

items.q: Can guinea pigs undergo surgery safely?
items.a: Yes. With proper anaesthesia and monitoring, many guinea pigs safely undergo surgery when medically necessary.

items.q: What is bumblefoot?
items.a: Bumblefoot is a painful infection of the feet caused by pressure sores, obesity, poor hygiene, or unsuitable cage flooring.

items.q: Why are my guinea pig's teeth becoming too long?
items.a: Abnormal tooth wear or dental disease can lead to overgrown teeth that interfere with eating.

items.q: How often should guinea pigs have veterinary check-ups?
items.a: Annual examinations are recommended, with more frequent visits for senior pets or those with chronic illnesses.

items.q: What foods should guinea pigs eat every day?
items.a: Good-quality hay, fresh vegetables rich in vitamin C, fresh water, and guinea pig-specific pellets are essential for good health.

items.q: Do you provide emergency treatment for guinea pigs?
items.a: Yes. Guinea pigs showing loss of appetite, breathing difficulty, severe weakness, urinary problems, or injuries should be examined immediately at our Pimple Nilakh clinic.
